editorial_description: Labs are deceptively low-maintenance — their short, dense double coat sheds year-round and goes into overdrive twice a year. Weekly brushing with a rubber curry brush or deshedding tool keeps loose fur under control and your furniture cleaner. Schedule a professional bath and nail trim every 8–12 weeks to stay ahead of that classic Lab smell and keep those powerful nails from clicking on hardwood.

Beagles have a short, tight coat that manages itself fairly well, but their long floppy ears are a hidden maintenance item — poor airflow makes them prone to wax buildup and infection. Brush weekly to manage moderate shedding, and clean those ears every 1–2 weeks with a vet-approved solution. A professional groom every 8–10 weeks keeps nails, ears, and coat in check without much fuss.

Boxers are one of the easiest breeds to groom — their short, smooth coat barely sheds and needs little more than a weekly rubdown with a grooming mitt to stay shiny. The main concern is nails, which grow quickly and can cause joint stress if left too long. A professional trim every 10–12 weeks keeps everything in order, and your Boxer will look sharp with almost no effort on your part.

The Doberman's sleek, close-lying coat is one of the lowest-maintenance in dogdom — a quick once-over with a soft cloth or rubber mitt every week keeps it gleaming. Because the coat is so thin, skin issues like dryness, irritation, or bumps are easy to spot and worth monitoring. Professional grooming every 10–12 weeks for a bath, nail trim, and skin check keeps your Doberman looking as sharp as they carry themselves.

Smooth-coat Dachshunds shed moderately and need a weekly brushing to stay tidy, while longhaired and wirehaired varieties demand more frequent attention to prevent tangles and matting. All Dachshunds have a propensity for dental disease, so regular tooth brushing at home and professional cleanings are important alongside routine grooming. Schedule a full groom every 8–10 weeks and don't let those little nails get too long — overgrown nails can worsen the back problems this breed is prone to.

Great Danes have a short, fine coat that requires minimal brushing — a rubber grooming glove once a week handles shedding just fine. What matters more with this gentle giant is keeping nails trimmed short, as the breed's size means overgrown nails put significant stress on joints and contribute to the gait problems that plague large dogs. Professional grooming every 10–12 weeks, ideally at a salon equipped for giant breeds, keeps your Dane comfortable and well-maintained.

The Poodle's dense, curly coat grows continuously and doesn't shed in the traditional sense — instead, loose hair tangles back into the coat and mats quickly without daily brushing. Professional trims are essential every 4–6 weeks to keep the coat manageable and free of painful mats, especially in high-friction areas like armpits and behind the ears. Poodles also grow hair inside their ear canals, which needs regular removal to prevent infections — a job best handled by your groomer.

The Bichon Frise has a soft, dense double coat that looks effortlessly fluffy but requires serious daily brushing to prevent the tight mats that form almost overnight. Professional grooming every 4–6 weeks is essentially non-negotiable for this breed — their coat doesn't maintain itself, and neglected mats can pull painfully on the skin. Pay special attention to the area under and around the eyes, which tends to stain from tear drainage and needs gentle daily wiping.

Goldendoodles can vary significantly in coat texture depending on which parent they take after, but most have wavy-to-curly coats that mat easily if not brushed several times a week. The areas most prone to tangling are behind the ears, under the collar, and in the armpits — these spots should be checked every few days. Professional grooming every 6–8 weeks keeps the coat at a manageable length and addresses the ear care that floppy, hair-filled ears require.

Labradoodle coats run the gamut from flat and Lab-like to tightly curled and Poodle-like, and your grooming schedule should match your individual dog's texture. Curlier coats mat faster and need brushing every other day, while wavy coats can get by with three or four times a week. All Labradoodles should see a professional groomer every 6–8 weeks, and their drop ears need regular inspection and cleaning to ward off moisture-related infections.

Cockapoos inherit the Poodle's tendency to mat, especially behind the ears and in the leg creases, making frequent brushing — ideally every other day — a must for keeping their soft, wavy-to-curly coats tangle-free. A slicker brush followed by a metal comb is the most effective combination for working through their dense fur without missing hidden knots. Professional grooming every 6–8 weeks keeps the coat looking its best and ensures ear health is monitored in those floppy ears.

German Shepherds are famously prolific shedders — their thick double coat blows out heavily twice a year and sheds moderately the rest of the time, earning them the nickname "German Shedder." Brushing three to four times a week with an undercoat rake or deshedding tool is the most effective way to manage loose fur before it migrates to every surface in your home. Professional grooming every 8–10 weeks, with a thorough deshed bath during coat-blow season, makes a dramatic difference in fur management.

Golden Retrievers have a beautiful double coat with long feathering on the chest, legs, and tail — and those feathered areas are mat magnets that need brushing several times a week to stay tangle-free. The dense undercoat sheds heavily, particularly in spring and fall, and regular deshedding sessions will save you considerable vacuuming. Professional grooming every 6–8 weeks keeps the coat properly trimmed and those pendulous ears clean and infection-free.

Siberian Huskies have a thick, self-cleaning double coat that sheds moderately year-round and "blows" its undercoat spectacularly twice a year — during these periods, daily raking is the only way to stay ahead of the fur. Huskies are naturally clean dogs that rarely need more than a few baths a year, and over-bathing can strip the natural oils that keep their coat healthy and weather-resistant. Professional grooming every 8–12 weeks, with extra sessions during coat-blow, is all this breed typically needs.

The Alaskan Malamute has an exceptionally thick double coat built for Arctic conditions, and it sheds prodigiously — brushing several times a week is the baseline, with daily grooming required during the twice-yearly blow-out. Never shave a Malamute: their double coat acts as insulation in both cold and hot weather, and shaving can permanently damage the coat's texture and regrowth. Professional grooming every 8–10 weeks, especially a thorough deshed bath with a high-velocity dryer, dramatically reduces shedding at home.

Both Pembroke and Cardigan Corgis have a medium-length double coat that sheds heavily — expect dog hair on everything and a real brush-out obligation of at least twice a week. During spring and fall coat blows, daily brushing is the only way to manage the volume of loose undercoat coming out. Professional grooming every 8–10 weeks keeps the coat tidy, and it's worth monitoring your Corgi's weight at each visit since this breed is prone to obesity that can stress their long backs.

The Shih Tzu's long, flowing double coat looks stunning but demands daily brushing to prevent the tangles that can develop overnight in their fine, silky fur. Many owners opt for a shorter "puppy cut" that's easier to maintain, but even clipped coats need brushing several times a week to stay mat-free. The hair around the Shih Tzu's large, prominent eyes needs daily wiping to prevent staining and eye irritation — and professional grooming every 4–6 weeks keeps everything beautifully trimmed.

Yorkshire Terriers grow hair rather than fur, giving them a fine, silky coat that behaves more like human hair than a typical dog coat — it grows continuously and tangles easily without daily brushing. The topknot (the hair on top of the head) needs regular maintenance to keep it out of the eyes, whether tied up or trimmed short. Yorkies are also prone to dental disease, so establishing a tooth-brushing routine at home between professional grooms every 4–6 weeks is an important part of their overall care.

The Maltese's pure white, silky coat is one of the most striking in the dog world — and one of the most demanding to maintain. Daily brushing is essential to prevent tangles in the fine, floor-length coat, and tear staining around the eyes is an ongoing challenge that requires gentle daily cleaning with a damp cloth or tear-stain solution. Professional grooming every 4–6 weeks keeps the coat pristine and is the best opportunity to address staining, ear care, and that characteristic topknot styling.

The Afghan Hound's long, luxurious coat is one of the most glamorous in the canine world — and among the most labor-intensive, requiring a dedicated daily brushing routine to prevent the deep tangles that can form quickly in that fine, flowing hair. High-quality conditioning is essential: the Afghan's coat is naturally fine and prone to dryness, and regular use of a leave-in conditioner helps brushing glide smoothly and prevents breakage. Professional grooming every 4–6 weeks is strongly recommended for keeping this show-stopper coat in peak condition.

The Havanese has a soft, silky double coat that grows long and mats easily, particularly in the areas of friction like behind the ears and under the legs. Brushing three to four times a week — more if the coat is kept long — is necessary to stay ahead of tangles, and a light detangling spray makes the process much easier. Professional grooming every 6–8 weeks keeps the coat at a manageable length and allows for thorough ear care, which this breed needs given its drop ears and hair growth in the ear canal.

The Miniature Schnauzer's distinctive look — boxy body, bushy brows, and flowing beard — requires consistent maintenance to keep it sharp. The wiry topcoat needs either hand-stripping (to preserve texture) or regular clipping, combined with weekly brushing of the furnishings (legs and beard) to prevent tangles. The beard is a particular focal point: it picks up food and moisture with every meal, so daily cleaning and a thorough professional groom every 6–8 weeks are the keys to keeping your Schnauzer looking properly dapper.

The Airedale Terrier is the "King of Terriers," and maintaining that regal coat requires the traditional technique of hand-stripping — removing dead outer coat by hand to preserve the wire texture that makes the breed water-resistant and distinctive. Clipping can be done for companion dogs, but it softens the coat texture over time and dulls the classic coloring. Professional grooming every 8–10 weeks with a groomer experienced in hand-stripping keeps an Airedale looking authentically Airedale, with ears checked and cleaned at each visit.

The Scottish Terrier's distinctive silhouette — low, long, and purposeful — is framed by a harsh, wiry topcoat over a dense, soft undercoat that gives the breed its weather-resistant character. Regular brushing keeps the undercoat from matting and the furnishings from tangling, while hand-stripping or tidying trims maintain the characteristic hard texture of the outer coat. Scotties can be prone to skin sensitivities, so professional grooming every 8–10 weeks is a good opportunity to check for any irritation under that thick coat.

The Wire Fox Terrier's tight, twisted outer coat requires hand-stripping to maintain the breed's classic hard texture — clipping softens the wire coat over time, which many terrier enthusiasts consider a disservice to the breed standard. Weekly brushing of the beard and leg furnishings prevents tangles in those softer areas, while the body coat needs stripping a few times a year to remove dead hair and encourage new growth. Professional grooming every 8–10 weeks with a terrier-savvy groomer is strongly recommended for keeping the Wire Fox Terrier looking its precise, athletic best.

The Chinese Crested's exposed skin requires the kind of daily attention you'd give your own skin — moisturizer to prevent dryness and cracking, and sunscreen before any outdoor time to protect against sunburn. The hairless variety still has a "crest" of hair on the head, paws, and tail that needs regular brushing and trimming, while the "Powderpuff" variety has a full soft coat requiring daily attention. Professional grooming every 4–6 weeks keeps skin health in check and ensures the crest and any coat are properly maintained.

The Xoloitzcuintli ("Xolo") is one of the world's oldest and rarest breeds, and their bare skin is as sensitive as it looks — prone to sunburn in summer and chill in winter, requiring protection year-round. Daily skin maintenance with a light, fragrance-free moisturizer and SPF-rated sunscreen for outdoor excursions is the foundation of Xolo care. Professional grooming every 4–6 weeks helps monitor skin condition and addresses nail care, which grows unnoticed without the covering of fur.

The American Hairless Terrier has smooth, warm-to-the-touch skin that shows off their athletic terrier build — and needs regular care since there's no coat to buffer the environment. Gentle weekly baths with a mild shampoo prevent oil buildup and keep the skin clear, while sunscreen protects against UV exposure during outdoor play. Professional grooming every 4–6 weeks is an ideal time to inspect the skin thoroughly for any signs of irritation, dryness, or unusual growths that might be missed at home.

French Bulldogs have a short, smooth coat that needs almost no brushing — a weekly wipe-down with a soft cloth or grooming mitt is enough to keep them looking tidy. The real grooming priority with Frenchies is their facial folds: the deep skin creases around the nose and under the eyes trap moisture and debris, creating a perfect environment for bacterial and yeast infections if not cleaned daily with a gentle wipe. Professional grooming every 8–10 weeks is a good opportunity for nail care and a thorough cleaning of all the wrinkled areas you might miss at home.

Bulldogs have a short, fine coat that requires minimal brushing, but their extensive facial wrinkles demand daily attention — trapped moisture in those folds leads quickly to skin fold dermatitis, a painful and smelly condition that's entirely preventable with regular cleaning. Use a damp cloth or unscented baby wipe to clean each fold daily and dry thoroughly, paying extra attention to the deep rope over the nose. Professional grooming every 8–10 weeks covers nail trims, a full-body bath, and a thorough wrinkle check from someone with a practiced eye.

Pugs shed far more than their small size suggests — their short, double-layer coat releases an impressive amount of fine hair year-round, so a weekly brushing with a rubber curry brush is the best way to stay on top of it. Their facial wrinkles need daily cleaning just like a Bulldog's, and their large, prominent eyes are prone to irritation and infection, requiring daily inspection and gentle wiping. Professional grooming every 8–10 weeks helps address the skin-fold hygiene and nail care that keeps a Pug comfortable.

Smooth-coat Chihuahuas need very little brushing — a gentle weekly once-over is enough to keep their fine coat shiny and remove loose hair. Long-coat Chihuahuas require more frequent brushing (two to three times a week) to prevent tangles in the soft, flowing fur around the ears, neck, and legs. Both varieties are highly prone to dental disease due to their tiny mouths and crowded teeth, making daily tooth brushing and professional dental care as important as any grooming routine; schedule a professional groom every 8–12 weeks.

Border Collies have a weather-resistant double coat that sheds moderately year-round and heavily during seasonal transitions, making brushing two to three times a week a necessity rather than a luxury. The rough-coat variety has longer fur that mats more readily in high-contact areas, while the smooth-coat variety is lower maintenance but still a dedicated shedder. Professional grooming every 8–10 weeks complements your at-home brushing routine — and a well-exercised, mentally stimulated Border Collie will stand still for it much more cooperatively.

Australian Shepherds have a gorgeous medium-length double coat with feathering on the legs and chest that mats easily if not brushed several times a week. Their thick undercoat sheds significantly in spring and fall, and regular deshedding sessions during these periods will save you considerable cleanup. Professional grooming every 8–10 weeks keeps the coat properly trimmed and those active, working-breed nails filed down to a healthy length.

The Bernese Mountain Dog's striking tricolor coat is thick and luxurious — and sheds heavily, requiring brushing several times a week to manage the volume of loose fur. The long outer coat tangles readily in the feathered areas of the chest, legs, and tail, so these spots deserve extra attention during your brushing sessions. Professional grooming every 6–8 weeks keeps the coat beautiful and the ears clean; given the breed's predisposition to joint issues, keeping nails short is especially important for maintaining healthy gait.

Newfoundlands have a massive, water-resistant double coat that was built for hauling fishing nets in the North Atlantic — which means it's thick, oily, and requires serious maintenance. Daily brushing is the ideal for this breed, and at minimum three to four times per week to prevent the mats that form quickly in such a dense coat. After bathing, a Newfie must be dried completely down to the skin — trapped moisture can cause hot spots and skin infections under all that coat, so a high-velocity dryer and patience are essential every 6–8 weeks.

The Cavalier's silky, medium-length coat has beautiful feathering on the ears, chest, legs, and tail that mats readily without regular brushing three to four times a week. Pay particular attention to behind the ears and under the legs, where friction and moisture create perfect conditions for knots. Professional grooming every 6–8 weeks keeps the silky coat at its flowing best and addresses the long, feathered ears that need regular cleaning to prevent the moisture-related infections Cavaliers are prone to.

English Springer Spaniels have a medium-length silky coat with heavy feathering on the ears, chest, and legs that picks up burrs, mud, and tangles on every outdoor adventure. Brushing three to four times a week is necessary to keep the feathered areas mat-free, with extra attention after field or trail outings. Professional grooming every 6–8 weeks keeps the coat trimmed and tidy, and their long, pendulous ears — which are prone to infection from poor airflow and moisture — deserve careful cleaning at every grooming appointment.

Rottweilers have a short, dense double coat that sheds moderately year-round and more heavily during seasonal changes — a weekly brushing with a rubber curry brush keeps loose hair under control and their naturally glossy coat looking sharp. Their floppy ears can trap moisture and debris, so check and clean them every couple of weeks. A professional bath and nail trim every 6–8 weeks keeps the basics covered; this is a wash-and-go breed that stays tidy with minimal effort.

The GSP's tight, athletic coat is built for field work — it repels water and dries fast, making it genuinely low-maintenance between professional appointments. Weekly brushing with a rubber mitt manages moderate shedding and keeps the coat gleaming. Their pendant ears are prone to moisture buildup after water activities, so clean them regularly; a professional groom every 6–8 weeks handles the rest.

Boston Terriers have a fine, minimal coat that barely sheds and needs only a quick weekly wipe-down with a grooming mitt to stay clean. The real maintenance priority is their facial folds — that distinctive tuxedo face comes with skin creases that trap moisture and can develop irritation or yeast if not cleaned every few days. A professional groom every 4–6 weeks keeps the fold areas, ears, and nails in good order.

The Belgian Malinois carries a practical, no-fuss short coat — dense enough to protect during active work but easy to maintain with a weekly brushing to manage moderate shedding. High-energy working dogs wear down their nails faster on hard surfaces, but Malis kept as companion dogs often need more frequent nail trims than owners expect. A professional bath and nail service every 8 weeks is all most Malinois need.

Dalmatians are deceptively heavy shedders — their short, fine white hairs embed themselves tenaciously into upholstery and clothing in a way that longer-coated breeds do not. Weekly brushing with a bristle brush or rubber curry mitt is essential to stay ahead of the constant shed cycle. Monthly baths help control shedding at its source; ear cleaning and nail trims round out a simple but consistent routine.

The Vizsla has one of the lowest-maintenance coats in dogdom — a close-lying, rust-gold coat that barely sheds and needs little more than a weekly wipe with a damp cloth or rubber mitt to stay gleaming. Their velvety coat does not hold dirt the way longer coats do, so baths are only needed every 8 weeks or when they have found something particularly memorable to roll in. The one area to watch is ears — Vizsla ears trap moisture, especially after water activities.

The Weimaraner's sleek silver-grey coat is almost self-maintaining — a quick weekly rub with a grooming glove removes loose hair and brings out that characteristic metallic shine with almost no effort. Like other drop-eared sporting breeds, their ears need regular inspection and cleaning to prevent moisture-related infections after outdoor and water activities. A professional bath, ear clean, and nail trim every 8 weeks keeps a Weimaraner looking as polished as they carry themselves.

Basset Hounds have a short, dense coat that manages itself well with weekly brushing, but their famously long ears are where the real maintenance work lies — poor airflow beneath those pendant ears creates a warm, moist environment that bacteria love. Clean ears every 1–2 weeks with a vet-approved cleaner and check for redness or odor between cleanings. A professional groom every 6–8 weeks covers bathing, nail care, and the ear attention this breed needs to stay comfortable.

Bloodhounds are a study in low-maintenance coat with high-maintenance anatomy — their short, smooth coat needs only weekly brushing, but those magnificent skin folds and pendulous ears demand consistent attention. Folds around the face and neck should be wiped out every few days to prevent moisture and bacterial buildup; ears need weekly cleaning because their extraordinary length traps debris and moisture with every step. A professional groom every 6–8 weeks rounds out the routine, but daily fold care is where Bloodhound health is won or lost.

The Chinese Shar-Pei's characteristic wrinkles are as demanding to maintain as they are distinctive — those deep folds trap moisture, food particles, and bacteria, and need to be cleaned and thoroughly dried every few days to prevent painful fold dermatitis. The coat itself is minimal care: a short, bristly texture that needs only a quick wipe-down or soft brush weekly. Schedule a professional groom every 4–6 weeks to keep folds, ears, and nails in shape, and seek out a groomer familiar with this breed's unique skin care needs.

The Basenji is often described as the cat of the dog world, and their grooming habits match — this breed obsessively self-grooms and has almost no dog odor, making them one of the cleanest-smelling breeds you will find. Their short, fine coat needs only a quick weekly wipe with a damp cloth or grooming mitt to remove loose hair. The main maintenance item is nails; a professional bath and nail service every 8–10 weeks keeps them comfortable without any major effort.

Jack Russell Terriers come in smooth and broken (rough) coat varieties — smooth coats need a quick weekly brush to manage light shedding, while broken coats benefit from occasional hand-stripping to maintain their texture and keep the characteristic wiry look. Both coat types are relatively low maintenance, but JRTs are energetic dogs whose nails can grow quickly, and dental disease is a common issue in small terriers worth staying ahead of. A professional groom every 6–8 weeks covers the basics; ask about hand-stripping if your JRT has a broken coat.

Akitas are famously fastidious self-groomers — they clean themselves almost like cats, and their naturally clean coat rarely develops a strong odor. But do not be lulled into complacency: this breed blows its coat spectacularly twice a year, filling your home with thick undercoat for several weeks at a time. Brush 2–3 times per week year-round and daily during coat blows; a professional deshedding bath every three months extracts what home brushing misses. Avoid frequent bathing as it strips the natural oils their double coat relies on.

The Chow Chow's lion-like double coat is one of the most voluminous in the dog world, and it requires serious commitment — brushing 2–3 times per week is essential to prevent the dense undercoat from matting, especially around the mane and hindquarters. Their deeply pigmented facial skin can also form folds around the eyes and muzzle that need regular cleaning to prevent irritation. Professional grooming every 6–8 weeks is strongly recommended; make sure your groomer has experience with double-coated breeds and uses a high-velocity dryer, as this coat holds water and takes a long time to dry thoroughly.

Pomeranians carry an impressive double coat for their tiny size — a thick, fluffy outer layer and a dense undercoat that requires daily brushing to stay mat-free and maintain its characteristic puffball silhouette. Without consistent daily brushing, the undercoat felts quickly, particularly behind the ears and under the legs. Beyond the coat, Pomeranians are prone to dental disease, so home tooth brushing and regular professional dental care matter alongside the every-4-6-week grooming appointments this breed needs.

Saint Bernards come in both short and long-coated varieties, but both carry a heavy, dense double coat that sheds prodigiously and requires brushing at least 2–3 times per week to stay manageable. The drool is a separate challenge entirely — Saint Bernards produce impressive amounts of it, and keeping the facial area and chest clean and dry is a daily task rather than a grooming-appointment task. A professional groom every 8 weeks handles the coat volume, nail care, and ear cleaning that this giant breed needs; find a groomer equipped for large dogs with ample drying capacity.

The Samoyed's brilliant white double coat is breathtaking and demanding in equal measure — daily brushing is non-negotiable to prevent matting in this high-volume coat, and seasonal coat blows twice a year push that commitment into multiple sessions per day. Despite the white color, the coat has a naturally non-staining quality, but regular professional baths every 8 weeks with a high-velocity dryer are essential for coat health. Dental care matters too; Samoyeds are prone to tooth issues, so build regular brushing at home into their routine alongside coat maintenance.

Shelties carry a luxurious double coat with flowing feathering on the chest, legs, and tail that is beautiful and prone to tangles in equal measure — brushing 2–3 times per week is essential to prevent mats from forming in the high-friction zones. They shed heavily year-round with dramatic coat blows twice a year, so investing in a good undercoat rake will save significant cleaning time at home. A professional groom every 6–8 weeks handles the detailed work; an experienced groomer can safely thin and tidy the feathering in ways that are difficult to replicate at home.

Like the Akita, the Shiba Inu is a naturally fastidious, almost catlike self-groomer who stays remarkably clean between baths. Their plush double coat is manageable with weekly brushing most of the year, but twice a year they blow their coat with remarkable intensity — budget for daily brushing during those 3–4 week shedding seasons. Professional bathing and deshedding every 8–10 weeks keeps the coat healthy; resist the urge to bathe more frequently as it disrupts the natural coat oils that keep a Shiba looking sharp.

Pembroke Welsh Corgis pack a surprising amount of double coat into a low-slung frame — their medium-length outer coat and thick undercoat shed consistently year-round and more heavily during seasonal changes. Weekly brushing with an undercoat rake or slicker brush keeps shedding manageable and prevents the fluffy pants (the feathering around their hindquarters) from developing tangles. A professional bath and deshed every 6–8 weeks makes a noticeable difference in your home's hair levels; nail care is worth particular attention as Corgis are prone to overgrowth.

The Flat-Coated Retriever's glossy, jet-black coat is one of the most striking in the sporting dog world — medium length with silky feathering on the ears, chest, legs, and tail that catches every briar and burr in the field. Brush 2–3 times per week to prevent tangles in the feathering and check thoroughly for debris after outdoor activities. Their drop ears need regular cleaning to prevent moisture buildup; a professional groom every 6–8 weeks keeps the coat trimmed, ears clean, and nails in order.

The Irish Setter's flowing chestnut-red coat is magnificent and requires real maintenance to stay that way — silky feathering on the ears, chest, belly, legs, and tail mats easily and needs brushing at least 2–3 times per week to stay tangle-free. Working dogs who spend time in the field will need post-adventure brushouts to remove seeds, burrs, and debris that embed in the feathering. Professional grooming every 6–8 weeks for a thorough bath, trim, and ear cleaning is recommended to maintain this breed's signature appearance.

The Old English Sheepdog's shaggy double coat is genuinely one of the most demanding in the dog world — this thick, coarse-outer, soft-inner coat mats at startling speed if daily brushing is skipped, and mats in a Bobtail coat can form down to the skin within days. The commitment here is real: 30–60 minutes of brushing per day is not unusual for owners keeping their dog in full coat. Professional grooming every 6–8 weeks with an experienced groomer is essential; many owners opt for a shorter utility trim which reduces at-home maintenance significantly while keeping the breed's characteristic charm.

Despite the spectacular butterfly-wing ears and flowing coat, Papillons are surprisingly manageable to groom — their single-layer silky coat has no undercoat to mat, so brushing 2–3 times per week is usually sufficient to keep it looking pristine. The ear fringe needs particular attention, as those dramatic feathers tangle easily and can obscure debris or early ear issues. A professional groom every 4–6 weeks keeps the coat trimmed, the ear fringe tidy, and the overall silhouette that makes this breed so elegant.

The Kerry Blue Terrier has a distinctive soft, wavy-to-curly coat that does not shed in the traditional sense — loose hair recycles back into the coat and requires regular brushing 2–3 times per week to prevent tangles and matting. The beard is a daily maintenance item, trapping food and moisture and needing a quick clean after every meal. Professional grooming every 6–8 weeks with a groomer experienced in terrier styling is recommended; the Kerry Blue's coat has a specific desired shape that requires practiced hands to achieve and maintain.

The Portuguese Water Dog's thick, curly coat is non-shedding in the same way a Poodle's is — loose hairs get caught in the curl rather than falling to the floor, which means regular brushing is essential to prevent those trapped hairs from matting. Brush thoroughly 2–3 times per week, paying extra attention to behind the ears and in the armpits where water and activity accelerate tangle formation. Professional grooming every 6–8 weeks keeps the coat in shape; their water-loving nature means ears need consistent post-swim cleaning to prevent infections.

Cocker Spaniels are one of the most beautiful and most maintenance-intensive breeds in the silky coat category — their long, flowing coat with heavy feathering on the ears, chest, belly, and legs requires daily brushing to prevent the rapid matting this coat type is known for. The long, pendulous ears sit right in the food and water bowls, stay perpetually damp, and are highly prone to ear infections; weekly ear cleaning is essential, not optional. Professional grooming every 4–6 weeks is necessary to maintain the Cocker's signature look and manage the coat volume.

The Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier's silky, wheat-colored coat is a standout feature of the breed — it is soft, low-shedding, and grows continuously, which means daily brushing is non-negotiable to prevent the tight mats this coat forms with alarming speed. The coat's texture changes significantly as a Wheaten matures from puppy to adult, and getting through that transition without severe matting requires committed grooming from an early age. Professional grooming every 6–8 weeks is recommended; ear health and dental care are secondary priorities worth keeping an eye on in this breed.

The Standard Schnauzer's signature look — bushy eyebrows, bristly moustache, and wiry salt-and-pepper coat — requires consistent professional maintenance to stay sharp. The wiry outer coat can be clipped for convenience (most companion dogs are) or hand-stripped to preserve its harsh texture and color; clipping gradually softens the coat over time but is entirely acceptable for non-show dogs. The beard needs daily cleaning after meals and water, as it traps food and moisture reliably; professional grooming every 5–8 weeks keeps the characteristic Schnauzer silhouette in order.
